Need to search first.I've written notes for all 23 verses, mostly from older and evangelical verse-by-verse commentaries. Three parts of your brief couldn't be met. The search tool hit its usage limit partway through, and every attempt to open a full page failed, so all notes come from the search-result extracts. Because of that I never reached Spurgeon on Psalm 52, the NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, or the Catholic and Orthodox sites (New Advent, catholic.com, OCA). No prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter came up either, so sections 3a and 3b are left out.

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1** (the cave of Adullam)
- **Guzik:** The name Adullam means "refuge," but God, not the cave, was David's real refuge. The cave was probably near where David killed Goliath, which shows how far he had fallen. He links the chapter to Psalms 142 and 57, both titled as written "in the cave." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-22/
- **Precept Austin:** Quotes Spurgeon and A. W. Pink that the cave made a good place to pray. Spurgeon is quoted saying that if David had prayed as much in his palace as in his cave, he might have avoided his later fall. Easton's Dictionary places the cave about 13 miles west of Bethlehem, in a hill full of caverns. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-22-commentary
- **Precept Austin also notes a contrast with the previous chapter:** there David leaned on people, lied to Ahimelech and pretended to be mad at Gath; here he turns to God alone. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-22-commentary

**v. 2** (the 400 distressed, indebted and discontented men)
- **Guzik:** These were not men David would have picked, but God called them to him. "Discontented" means "bitter of soul" in Hebrew. They came when David was hunted and despised. He made them a disciplined band, not a mob, and refused to turn them against Saul. They became the "mighty men" of 1 Chronicles 12:8. Like Spurgeon, he reads this as a picture of Christ gathering the spiritually broken. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-22/ ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-1Sa/1Sa-22.cfm
- **Spurgeon ("Recruits for the King"):** David in the cave is a type (a foreshadowing) of Christ, rejected by the world. He applies the three groups to sinners: the distressed have nothing left, and the debtors owe God a debt they cannot pay, which Christ pays as their substitute. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons62.xli.html
- **Spurgeon elsewhere:** Christ, "the great Antitype," gathers spiritual bankrupts as David did (https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons58/sermons58.xvii.html). David's first band looked disreputable to Saul's government, and the Son of David still receives sinners (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/open-house-for-all-comers).
- **Precept Austin:** One writer it quotes connects the debts to Saul's heavy taxes and compares the distress to what drove the Prodigal Son home. It also quotes the point that God likes to work through people the world thinks unfit, such as Jacob and Moses. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-22-commentary

**v. 3** (Mizpeh of Moab)
- **Why Moab:** Commentators agree that Jesse was the grandson of Ruth the Moabitess, and that Moab was Saul's enemy (1 Samuel 14:47). Barnes, JFB, Poole and Benson all make these points. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/22-3.htm
- **Where Mizpeh was:** The name means "watchtower." Barnes and Ellicott suggest Zophim, on top of Pisgah. Whedon names Kerak as one option but prefers a high point like Nebo or Pisgah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/22-3.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/1-samuel-22.html
- **"Till I know what God will do for me":** Ellicott says David's old trust had returned. He notes David says "God" (Elohim) rather than the LORD's personal name when speaking to a foreign king, which he puts down to reverence. Benson and Matthew Henry see a son's tender care and full surrender to God's will. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/22-3.htm
- **Constable:** David may also have wanted Moab's support in case Saul's hostility became open war. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-3.html
- **Guzik:** David knew he was anointed to be king but not how God would bring it about, so he had to trust without knowing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-22/

**v. 4** (the parents stay in Moab)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The parents had fled Bethlehem and were too old for life on the run. It takes "while David was in the hold" to cover the whole period of wandering up to Hebron, not just the fort in Moab. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-22.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/22.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** Children should honour their parents and look after their comfort. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/22-3.htm

**v. 5** (the prophet Gad)
- **Where the advice came from:** Ellicott and JFB say it came from God, not just Gad's own good sense. Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary guess that Samuel sent Gad. The Pulpit says that if David had stayed in Moab he probably would never have become king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/22-5.htm
- **Why go back to Judah:** Poole and Gill say David should show himself openly in his own tribe, both to stake his claim and to show he was innocent and trusted God. The Cambridge Bible says he needed to build a reputation through deeds such as rescuing Keilah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/22-5.htm
- **Guzik:** Saul had resisted the prophets, while David received God's word. David had to learn to trust God in the middle of danger. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-22/
- **Bob Deffinbaugh (bible.org):** Gad's sudden appearance is like Melchizedek's. Judah would be the first tribe to accept David (2 Samuel 2:4). Hereth was David's "Sherwood Forest." https://bible.org/seriespage/saul-loses-his-grip-1-samuel-225-2314
- **Where Hereth was:** Unknown, according to Barnes. The Cambridge Bible suggests Kharas, near Keilah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/22-5.htm

**v. 6** (Saul under the tamarisk)
- **Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary:** Saul was holding formal court in the open, with his spear in hand as a sceptre. Ellicott notes that Saul's darkest decision was made in the spot he loved. JFB and Benson say early kings carried a spear instead of a sceptre. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/22-6.htm
- **Bible Hub Q&A:** A tamarisk also stands at both ends of Saul's story, since he is later buried under one (1 Samuel 31:13). It reads the scene as showing a king who was stuck in place and anxious, while David kept moving. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_was_Saul_under_the_tamarisk_tree.htm

**v. 7** ("men of Benjamin")
- **Keil & Delitzsch and Coffman:** Saul had filled his court with men from his own tribe and rewarded them well. He was warning them that a king from Judah would favour Judah instead. Coffman adds that Saul never really tried to unite all the tribes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-samuel-22.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-8.html
- **Guzik:** Saul appealed to the worst in his men. He called David "the son of Jesse," the humblest name he could find. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-22/

**v. 8** (Saul's accusation)
- **Guzik:** Saul was paranoid and self-pitying, and led by guilt and accusation. Jonathan had never done what Saul claimed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-22/
- **Constable:** There is no evidence Jonathan encouraged an ambush. **Gill:** Saul only suspected the covenant, since only Jonathan and David knew about it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-8.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Saul's "none of you is sorry for me" was meant to work on their feelings and push them to act. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_022.cfm

**v. 9** (Doeg speaks)
- **Gill:** Doeg hated David, wanted Saul's favour and promotion, and spoke before anyone else could. Josephus calls him a Syrian. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-9.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Doeg may have spoken only because Saul forced the issue. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_022.cfm
- **The Biblical Illustrator:** Notes that Herod was also an Edomite, and warns that there is always "a Doeg looking on." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-9.html
- **Cambridge Bible and Psalm 52:** Psalm 52 is titled as written about this event. Doeg had a "false tongue" because, although his facts were true, he used them to confirm Saul's false suspicion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/22-9.htm

**v. 10** (the report)
- **Guzik:** Doeg moved Saul's anger away from Saul's own staff and onto the priests. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/1-samuel/1-samuel-22.cfm
- **Gill:** Doeg's report was true but deceptive, because he left out that David had tricked the priest. Gill also gives a Jewish view: asking God by Urim and Thummim was done for a king, not a private person, so Doeg was in effect accusing David of claiming the throne. https://studylight.org/commentaries/spa/geb/1-samuel-22.html (Spanish translation of Gill)

**v. 11** (all the priests summoned)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Saul sent for every priest at Nob, as though he had already planned the massacre. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/22.htm

**v. 12** ("Here I am, my lord")
- **Matthew Henry:** Calling the high priest just "son of Ahitub" was a deliberate insult. Ahimelech's reply shows a man ready to hear the charge because he knew he had done nothing wrong. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-6.html

**v. 13** (the charge)
- **Guzik:** Saul kept up his reckless paranoia, imagining both a conspiracy and an ambush. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-22/

**v. 14** (Ahimelech defends David)
- **Constable:** Ahimelech pleaded for David much as Jonathan had earlier. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-20.html
- **Bridgeway Bible Commentary:** Ahimelech says he helped David out of loyalty to Saul, believing David was on the king's business. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-8.html

**v. 15** ("Was that the first time?")
- **Clarke:** Asking God for David was nothing new, and Ahimelech probably knew of no quarrel between David and Saul. He treated David as the king's son-in-law. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-15.html
- **Guzik:** Ahimelech told the exact truth. He had questioned David closely (21:1), but David lied to him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-22/

**v. 16** (the sentence)
- **Matthew Henry:** The sentence was rushed, with no time for defence, and it fell on Ahimelech's whole family although no charge was made against them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-15.html
- **Constable:** This time Saul would not listen to reason. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-20.html

**v. 17** (the guards refuse)
- **Guzik:** The servants feared God more than Saul. Saul had been reluctant to destroy God's enemies (15:9) but not to kill God's priests. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-22/
- **Precept Austin:** Saul's added words, "priests *of the LORD*," show his "godless audacity." https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-22-commentary
- **Constable:** The soldiers respected the priesthood and probably saw that the order was irrational. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-9.html

**v. 18** (Doeg kills 85 priests)
- **The linen ephod:** One note on Bible Hub's compiled page (unnamed in the extract) says the priests probably came dressed in their white robes of office, which makes the deed worse. Henry says they were of serving age, 20 to 50. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/22-18.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-15.html
- **Why the text keeps saying "Edomite":** Benson says it clears Israel of the butchery and explains Doeg's readiness, since his nation hated Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/22-18.htm
- **Barnes:** Doeg did not necessarily kill them all with his own hand. Gill notes the Septuagint and Josephus give higher numbers, and Josephus says others helped him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-18.html
- **Eli's house:** Matthew Henry and Coffman see this as the fulfilment of the judgment announced against Eli's family (1 Samuel 2:27–36). Henry adds that God was righteous in allowing what Saul did unrighteously. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_022.cfm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-18.html

**v. 19** (Nob destroyed)
- **Constable:** Saul failed to wipe out the Amalekites when God commanded it, yet wiped out Nob with no command from God. Doeg went beyond his orders, though Saul stayed responsible. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-8.html
- **William Kelly:** "The man who spared the Amalekites" destroyed the priests without mercy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-20.html
- **Matthew Henry:** He calls it barbarous cruelty. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-18.html

**v. 20** (Abiathar escapes)
- **Bible Hub Q&A:** Abiathar's escape fits the earlier promise in 1 Samuel 2:33 that one would be spared. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_Saul_kill_priests_in_1_Sam_22_18.htm ; https://biblehub.com/q/1_Sam_22_18_God_s_justice_mercy.htm
- **Constable:** From now on the priesthood was with David rather than Saul. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-20.html
- **Kelly:** Both priest and prophet were now with God's chosen king. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-20.html

**v. 21** (the news reaches David)
- **Constable:** Saul was still responsible for the massacre, even though Doeg did the killing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-8.html

**v. 22** (David takes responsibility)
- **Guzik:** David meant it in two ways. His mere presence made Ahimelech look guilty, which no one could have prevented. His lie also left the priest exposed and robbed him of the chance to take sides knowingly and die with more honour. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-22/
- **Constable:** David admitted his deception led to the slaughter. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-20.html
- **Gill (summary):** David saw himself as the cause of the disaster. https://studylight.org/commentaries/spa/geb/1-samuel-22.html
- **Talmud:** The Bible Hub compilation cites a saying from the Talmud tract Sanhedrin in which David is blamed for the priests' deaths, for Doeg's ruin, and for the deaths of Saul and his sons. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/22-18.htm

**v. 23** ("You will be safe with me")
- **Constable:** David became protector of the priesthood, and the future king and the future priest were now fugitives together. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-20.html
- **Guzik:** David could not undo the deaths, but he admitted his guilt and cared for the one survivor. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-22/

---

## 2. Where interpreters differ

None of the disagreements I found split along denominational lines. They are differences between individual commentators, whose traditions are noted below where the sources give them.

- **v. 10, did Doeg lie?** Gill (Baptist) reports that some read Psalm 52:3 to mean Doeg made up the claim that Ahimelech asked God for David. Gill himself thinks it happened. Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran) say it certainly happened, since Ahimelech does not deny it in v. 15. https://studylight.org/commentaries/spa/geb/1-samuel-22.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/22-9.htm
- **v. 9, Doeg's rank:** Keil & Delitzsch take him to be marshal of the court. The Pulpit Commentary (Anglican) calls the KJV's "set over the servants" "entirely wrong" and says he was simply standing among them. The Septuagint, as JFB reports, has him over Saul's mules. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/22-9.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/22.htm
- **v. 22, how guilty was David?** Guzik and Constable focus on David's lie. Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) instead says David's mistake was letting Doeg go, and that he should have killed him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-22/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/22-18.html
- **v. 18, God's role:** Henry and the Bible Hub Q&A stress that God allowed this to fulfil the judgment on Eli, while Saul still carried the blame. The Pulpit Commentary adds that the evil a family does affects later generations (Exodus 20:5). https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_Saul_kill_priests_in_1_Sam_22_18.htm ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-22.html

## 3. Other views

I couldn't reach the modern-scholarship, Catholic or Orthodox sites (see the top). The only related item found: Bible Hub's Catholic page for v. 18 gives the Douay-Rheims and New American Bible translations, but no commentary. https://biblehub.com/catholic/1_samuel/22-18.htm
